introduction_markdown: Duration: Three Hours. Answer BOTH questions in SECTION A and ONE EACH from SECTIONS B and C in the SAME Answer Booklet, beginning each section on a new page. Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks. Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty. In the SUMMARY question, use mainly your own words. Indiscriminate copying of portions of the passage as your answer will earn you little or no marks. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. A pre-prepared or memorised composition will earn you little or no marks.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**SECTION B: COMPOSITION (20 marks)**

Mark distribution: Content and Organisation (06 marks); Expression (08 marks); Accuracy (06 marks).

Choose ONE topic to write about from the list below. You are advised to write clearly and effectively, to spell and punctuate correctly, and to ensure that your writing is appropriate in style and content to the topic chosen. Avoid obscene language and do not disclose your identity. You should write between 500 and 550 words.

questions.corrige_markdown:
**Plan**

1. Introduction: definition and scope of violence.
2. Forms of violence (physical, verbal, psychological, cyber).
3. Causes (poverty, family example, media, drugs, injustice, intolerance).
4. Consequences (deaths, economic loss, displacement, revenge).
5. Solutions (family, school, government, media, leaders) and conclusion.

**Model composition (528 words)**

Violence, which may be defined as the deliberate use of physical force or power to hurt, frighten or control other people, is one of the most worrying problems of our time. It is found in homes, in schools, on the streets and, at its worst, in wars between and within nations. Because it destroys lives and slows down development, every responsible citizen must understand its causes, its effects and the ways of overcoming it.

Violence takes many forms. The most visible is physical: fights between students, armed robbery, assaults on women and children, and political clashes. There is also verbal and psychological violence, such as threats, insults and bullying, which wounds the mind even when it leaves no mark on the body. In our era, one may add cyber violence, where hateful messages spread rapidly on social media and can ruin a person's reputation within hours.

The causes are equally varied. Poverty and unemployment push frustrated young people towards crime, while children who grow up watching their parents quarrel and beat one another often learn to settle disputes with their fists. Films and video games that glorify guns and fighting also play a part, as does the abuse of alcohol and drugs, which weakens self-control. On a larger scale, injustice, corruption and the denial of rights drive people to take up arms, and ethnic or religious intolerance can turn small disagreements into bloody confrontations.

The consequences are tragic. First, violence kills and cripples. Families lose their breadwinners, and survivors carry scars, both physical and emotional, for the rest of their lives. Second, it ruins the economy: shops are looted, farms abandoned, schools closed and investors frightened away. Third, it displaces people. Thousands of families in troubled regions of the world have fled their homes and live in camps or with relatives, where their children miss years of schooling. Finally, violence breeds more violence, because victims who receive no justice may seek revenge, and the circle never ends.

Fortunately, solutions exist. The home must come first, since parents who correct their children with patience, explain instead of beating and set a good example raise peaceful adults. Schools should teach conflict resolution, and clubs for debate, music and sport can channel the energy of young people into positive activities. The government, for its part, must provide jobs, enforce the law fairly and punish offenders whatever their rank, because impunity encourages crime. The media have the duty to promote peace instead of hatred, and religious and traditional leaders can use their influence to preach dialogue and forgiveness. Neighbouring communities may form vigilance committees that work closely with the police, but they must never take the law into their own hands.

In conclusion, violence is a disease that feeds on ignorance, injustice and fear. It cannot be cured by force alone, since force only deepens the wound. A lasting remedy requires education, fairness and dialogue, and each of us can contribute by refusing to hit, to insult or to applaud those who do. If we choose understanding over aggression in our daily lives, we will build a society where disputes are settled with words and where every person can live without fear.

**Marking grid**

| Criterion | Marks | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Content and Organisation | 6 | Ideas relevant to the topic, developed with convincing detail, in well-planned paragraphs with an introduction and a conclusion |
| Expression | 8 | Varied and precise vocabulary, varied sentence structures, a register suited to the type of composition, fluent links between paragraphs |
| Accuracy | 6 | Correct grammar, tenses, spelling and punctuation, with very few errors |

**Common mistakes**

1. Writing only about one form of violence (war) when the topic is general; the essay needs a clear plan.
2. Listing causes and effects as bare points without examples or explanation, or finishing without a conclusion.
